parts.partTitle: Why JSON Fails at Kafka Scale

beats.headline: Is JSON destroying your Kafka performance?
beats.subline: Stop treating events like text files. Here is why high-scale pipelines demand binary schemas.
beats.narration: JSON is great for debugging, but it is a disaster for high-throughput Kafka. Every field name is repeated in every message, inflating your storage and network egress by up to 75 percent.

beats.title: Payload Bloat: JSON vs Avro
beats.narration: JSON repeats every key as ASCII text. Avro is purely binary. It uses zig-zag encoding for numbers and omits field names entirely, saving massive bandwidth and reducing GC pressure on your JVM.

beats.title: Avro Schema Resolution
beats.subtitle: How the consumer decodes raw bytes
beats.narration: Because Avro bytes lack field identifiers, you need the writer schema to decode them. The consumer resolves the writer schema against its own reader schema, filling missing fields with defaults.

beats.title: The Avro .avsc Contract

steps.explanation: No more guessing if a number is an int or long.
Must place null first to match the default value.

beats.narration: Define your contract in an avsc file. Note the union type for optional fields: null must come first to match the default. This is the source of truth that prevents breaking changes.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: JSON repeats keys; Avro is binary
Avro uses schema resolution for evolution
Always put null first in union types

beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we look at the 5-byte wire format and how the Schema Registry acts as a gatekeeper for your event contracts.

beats.headline: Why does every Avro message start with 5 bytes?
beats.subline: It is not just a header—it is the secret to decoupling your producers and consumers.
beats.narration: You cannot embed a 1KB schema in every message. The Confluent wire format solves this by prepending a tiny 5-byte header to every payload.

beats.title: The 5-Byte Header Anatomy
beats.subtitle: Magic byte + 4-byte Schema ID
beats.narration: Byte zero is the magic byte. Bytes one through four are the Schema ID. The consumer reads this ID, fetches the schema from the registry once, and caches it in memory.

beats.title: Registry Caching Logic
beats.caption: Avoid the registry as a bottleneck

lines.text: No HTTP calls for steady-state traffic

beats.narration: The registry is not a single point of failure. Once the producer or consumer resolves an ID, it is cached in the JVM. Only new schemas trigger an HTTP call.

beats.title: Subjects & Naming
beats.narration: Use TopicNameStrategy for simple pipelines. If your topic carries multiple event types, switch to RecordNameStrategy to keep your schema subjects clean and organized.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Registry is cached in-memory per JVM

beats.narration: Registry caching keeps your pipeline fast. In Part 3, we cover compatibility modes that stop breaking changes at the CI/CD gate.

beats.headline: How to stop breaking changes before production?
beats.subline: Schema Registry is your automated gatekeeper. Here is how to configure your safety net.
beats.narration: Breaking a consumer in production is a nightmare. Schema Registry compatibility modes block incompatible changes during your CI/CD build, failing the pipeline before code ever reaches the broker.

beats.title: Compatibility Modes
beats.narration: Backward compatibility lets new consumers read old data. Full transitive is the gold standard, checking your new schema against every historical version to ensure total safety.

beats.title: CI/CD Compatibility Gate
beats.subtitle: Fail fast, deploy safely
beats.narration: Run compatibility tests in your CI pipeline. If a change violates your mode, the registry returns a 409 error, forcing the developer to fix the schema before merging.

beats.title: Maven Plugin Setup
beats.caption: Generate type-safe Java classes
beats.narration: Use the avro-maven-plugin to generate Java classes. Always set stringType to String to avoid Utf8 objects, and use SpecificRecord to get type-safe getters for your decimals and timestamps.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Spring Boot integration and final tips →
beats.narration: Compatibility is your best defense. In Part 4, we wrap it all up with Spring Boot configuration and the final production-grade patterns.

beats.headline: Stop casting objects in your Kafka listeners.
beats.subline: Here is how to wire up Avro with Spring Boot for production-ready, type-safe messaging.
beats.narration: Stop using GenericRecord and manual casting. With proper Spring configuration, your Kafka listeners can inject generated Avro classes directly.

beats.title: Spring Kafka Configuration
beats.code:
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      value-serializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer
    consumer:
      properties:
        specific.avro.reader: true
        auto.register.schemas: false

steps.explanation: Use the Confluent serializer for the 5-byte header.
Crucial: injects your generated class, not GenericRecord.

beats.narration: Set specific dot avro dot reader to true. This forces Spring to use your generated classes. Disable auto-register schemas in production to ensure your CI/CD pipeline remains the only source of truth.

beats.title: Type-Safe Listener

steps.explanation: Directly inject your generated Avro class.
Logical types handle decimal precision automatically.

beats.narration: Your listener is now clean and type-safe. Logical types like decimal and timestamp-millis are automatically converted to BigDecimal and Instant, eliminating manual parsing errors.

beats.title: Avro vs Protobuf
beats.narration: Choose Avro for data-heavy streaming and analytical pipelines. Choose Protobuf if you need to share the same definitions across gRPC services and Kafka topics.

beats.title: Chapter Complete!
takeaways: Use Avro for data, Protobuf for APIs
